# Schema changes during a live sync

> How sluice keeps a running sync online while the source schema evolves — what forwards automatically, what refuses loudly, and how to recover.

A source schema rarely stands still. Columns get added, types get widened, indexes come and go while a continuous sync is running. sluice does not manage those migrations for you — tools like Atlas, sqitch, Flyway, and liquibase do that — but it does keep the stream online through them. By default it forwards the operator's own committed DDL onto the target, so a routine ALTER TABLE no longer wedges the sync. This page covers what forwards automatically, the narrow set of changes that still refuse loudly, and the drained-migrate recovery when one does.

Fixed in v0.156.10 (GC-44): a column type change the stream did not see was rounded into the target, at exit 0. Forwarding classifies each source schema change against the last shape it saw for the table. After a warm resume, a restart, a sync run leg restart or an automatic retry after a transient error it had seen nothing, so the table's first schema boundary — a change made while the stream was stopped, or after it restarted and before the table's next row — was cached as the new baseline and never applied to the target; the ADR-0091 seed guard skipped the same shape at the first boundary after a cold start. A type widen within its family left the target's narrow column in place, and every following value was rounded into it: DATETIME → DATETIME(6), DECIMAL(10,2) → DECIMAL(12,4), FLOAT → DOUBLE, or a Postgres timestamp or numeric precision. Measured on MySQL 8.0 in file/pos and GTID mode, MariaDB 11.4, Postgres 16 and vttestserver; a VARCHAR widen or an ADD COLUMN failed loudly at the next row instead. Separately, on a running Postgres-source stream, timestamp(0) → timestamp(6) (and the same for timestamptz, time and timetz) classified as no change and was never forwarded, so every later value was rounded to whole seconds (GC-44 F3). Each table's first boundary after a start is now checked against the target (RESUME-SCHEMA-DIVERGENCE), and streams that forward no DDL now check every boundary (SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED). A drop (or a nullability, CHECK, index or rename change) that is the first schema change on a table after a cold start is not forwarded and is logged at WARN; a type change there is checked against the target and forwarded if genuine.

- Affected releases: v0.99.45 through v0.156.9 with forwarding on (the default); from v0.79.0 with the opt-in --forward-schema-add-column; from v0.73.1 under --inject-shard-column (coordinated Shape A). The Postgres (0) → (6) case: v0.99.176 through v0.156.9. For streams that forward no DDL see below.

- Who was exposed: a stream whose synced table had a column type changed while it was stopped, or between a restart and that table's next change (a sync run leg restart and an automatic retry count), or right after its cold start.

- Upgrading does not repair rows already rounded, and one check works only before the upgrade. Before upgrading, run sluice schema diff and compare each target column's declared type with the source's; where the source's is wider, the rows written since the change hold rounded values, and the table needs a re-copy. If you already upgraded, the first start applied the difference itself, so a later diff is clean and proves nothing: grep that first post-upgrade start's log for forwarding the difference (target-witnessed, GC-44). Every hit whose difference= names a type change marks a column whose earlier rows were rounded; re-copy that table. For the Postgres (0) → (6) case the target column is still (0): alter it, then re-copy the table or the affected rows.

Fixed in v0.158.0: three CRITICAL silent-data defects in CDC, and a HIGH one in forwarding. Each left wrong values on a target or in a backup chain at exit 0. No sluice check can clear an affected target or chain with certainty: backup verify (both depths) and a restore read a chain that is internally consistent, sluice verify --depth=sample reaches only a sample of rows (and before v0.158.1 hashed each side's columns in its own declared order, so it read a column swap as clean), and across engines verify compares row counts only (what verify cannot see). The fixes refuse where sluice cannot prove a shape, so some DDL that used to stream through now stops the stream: see COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED, multi-column ALTERs and decoding rows behind the head.

- A MySQL/MariaDB binlog stream behind the head decoded earlier rows under the wrong column names (CRITICAL, Bug 301). The reader took a table's column list from information_schema, which answers as of now, while decoding events recorded earlier. A change that kept the column count and every column's type family — a reorder of same-type columns, a column-name swap, a same-type drop-and-add, an ENUM label reorder — decoded with values under the wrong names (or the other label). Affected: every release since v0.1.0, for every backup incremental and backup stream window, every warm-resumed sync start, the CDC phase after a cold copy, and a live sync that lagged; at the head too, for a change issued from another default database (USE other; ALTER TABLE app.t …). From v0.113.0 cross-family and count-changing shapes refused loudly; same-family ones stayed silent through v0.157.2. What to do: set binlog_row_metadata=FULL on the source first (MySQL: SET PERSIST binlog_row_metadata = 'FULL'; MariaDB: SET GLOBAL binlog_row_metadata = 'FULL' plus binlog_row_metadata = FULL under [mariadbd]), then re-snapshot each affected sync target (sync start --restart-from-scratch) and rebuild each affected chain from a new backup full.

- A MariaDB source on its default binlog_row_metadata=NO_LOG streamed UNSIGNED integers above the signed maximum as negative numbers (CRITICAL, MARIADB-NOLOG-UNSIGNED). NO_LOG records no signedness, and the decoder read such integers as signed: BIGINT UNSIGNED 18446744073709551615 arrived as -1. A Postgres target stored the negative value; an UPDATE or DELETE keyed by such a value matched no row and was dropped. Affected: v0.99.271 through v0.157.2, on sync start's CDC phase, backup incremental, backup stream and sync from-backup applying those chains. Not affected: MySQL 8.0/8.4, MariaDB under MINIMAL or FULL, PlanetScale and Vitess, every cold copy and migrate, and DECIMAL/FLOAT/DOUBLE/YEAR/BIT columns. How to check a Postgres target: SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE col < 0 for each column the source declares UNSIGNED; any hit is proof. A lost update or delete leaves no trace on the target. What to do: re-snapshot the target (sync start --restart-from-scratch) and rebuild chains from a new backup full. If you cannot upgrade yet, SET GLOBAL binlog_row_metadata = 'MINIMAL' (and in the option file) makes binlog written afterwards decode correctly on older releases; binlog already written is not fixed.

- A column RENAME swap on the source left the target's existing rows under the wrong column names (CRITICAL, RENAME-SWAP-FORWARD). RENAME COLUMN b TO c, RENAME COLUMN c TO b (or a rotation) reached the target as no change, measured on MySQL 8.0 and Postgres 16, so every pre-swap row the source never touched again stayed swapped. Affected: every release of sync start (from v0.79.0 opt-in and v0.99.45 by default the forward path read the swap as no change), --inject-shard-column since v0.73.0, and chain restore and sync from-backup in every release that replays a schema delta; MySQL, MariaDB and Postgres sources alike. How to check: run sluice verify --depth=sample with v0.158.1 or later: it compares columns by name, so a swapped target mismatches on every sampled row that predates the swap. v0.158.0 and older hashed each side's columns in its own declared order and read a swapped target as clean, so a clean result from them does not clear it. A sample samples: when the pre-swap rows are a small fraction of the table, raise --sample-rows-per-table, or compare the affected columns' values by primary key between source and target yourself. Re-copy the table where they differ.

- Two or more columns changing type or nullability in one ALTER were forwarded as no change (HIGH, silent on a Postgres target). A Postgres target kept the old type and rounded every later value (numeric(10,2) kept for two columns widened to numeric(12,4): 1.2345 landed as 1.23); a MySQL target refused the first value that did not fit. Affected: the forward path from v0.99.45, and --inject-shard-column since v0.73.0. How to check: compare the target's column types with the source's for any table altered this way while a stream ran, and re-copy a table whose values were rounded.

Fixed in v0.159.0: a CRITICAL and two HIGH silent-data defects in CDC. Each left the target with merged or misplaced rows at exit 0. Upgrading does not repair rows already affected. The fixes add refusals that change behaviour: see COLUMN-IDENTITY-CHANGED and KEY-COLLATION-*.

- A MySQL/MariaDB schema change that left a column name holding a different column was invisible (CRITICAL, RENAME-SWAP-INVISIBLE). DROP COLUMN c, ADD COLUMN c of the same type, RENAME COLUMN c TO tmp, ADD COLUMN c, DROP COLUMN b, RENAME COLUMN c TO b, or a rename swap whose order a MODIFY … AFTER restored before the table's next row produced no schema boundary, so the target kept every existing row's old values under the reused name — at the head and on a warm resume, under MINIMAL and FULL alike. Affected: not bisected; treat every release through v0.158.1 as affected, on sync start, backup incremental/backup stream chains and sync from-backup. How to check: run sluice verify --depth sample on v0.159.0 (it compares columns by name since v0.158.1). A target that lacks a source column (the tmp shape) fails as COLUMN-MISMATCH deterministically; for the other shapes each sampled pre-change row whose reused column differs mismatches, so raise --sample-rows-per-table where few rows predate the change. A clean sample is evidence, not proof. The default --depth count cannot see it. What to do: re-copy each affected table (sync start --reset-target-data --yes) and rebuild affected chains from a new backup full.

- A key column's collation or character-set change merged distinct source rows into one target row (HIGH, KEY-COLLATION-FIRST-BOUNDARY). After, for example, MODIFY k … COLLATE utf8mb4_bin on a key that was utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci (or PAD SPACE → NO PAD, or utf8mb4 → ascii_bin), a new row distinct only under the new collation ('A' beside 'a', 'a ' beside 'a') merged into the existing one: on a PRIMARY KEY the existing row vanished, on a UNIQUE column it was overwritten. It happened when the stream met the change as the first schema boundary of a run (a warm resume, or a live stream's first boundary after its cold start), on every --schema-changes=refuse stream, in every chain restore, and on a Postgres source on every entry, because pgoutput carries no collation. Also with no schema change at all: a MySQL 8 → MariaDB stream whose utf8mb4_0900_* key holds values differing only by trailing spaces, and a Postgres → MySQL-family stream with a UNIQUE key (beside the primary key) on the database default collation holding values differing only in case. Affected: not bisected; treat every release through v0.158.1 as affected. How to check: in the measured cases each merge left the target one row short, so sluice verify on a quiesced stream reports a count mismatch. To find candidate collisions, group each key column on the source under the target's collation: on MySQL, SELECT k COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci AS kk, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY kk HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; on Postgres, GROUP BY k COLLATE "<target collation>", or lower(k) as an approximation for a case-insensitive MySQL target. What to do: re-copy each table that mismatches.

- A FULL-metadata row held to an earlier shape was not compared on collation (HIGH, DEFERRED-KEY-COLLATION). Under binlog_row_metadata=FULL, a key's collation change folded behind a later retype or drop let a row merge on the target before the stream refused with RESUME-SCHEMA-DIVERGENCE, and that refusal's remedy left the merge in place. Affected: v0.158.0 and v0.158.1. What to do: check and re-copy as in the previous item.

Fixed in v0.159.1: copies that merged rows, Postgres keys the v0.159.0 guard left unchecked, and older binaries restoring a key-collation window. Upgrading does not repair rows that already merged. The fixes add refusals: see KEY-COLLATION-*. One HIGH issue in chain restore was still open in this release (below); v0.159.2 fixed it for MySQL and MariaDB binlog sources (v0.159.2 notice).

- A copy that upserts merged two source rows whose keys the target's collation equates (HIGH, KEY-COLLATION-ROWWRITER). v0.159.0 guarded the CDC appliers, but the copy phase's idempotent writer still upserted unchecked. That writer serves schema add-table, a resumed or chunk-resumed copy, --force-cold-start, the VStream COPY and restore of a rotated chain. Where the target key's collation equates two values the source keeps apart ('A' and 'a' on a _ci key from a _bin source, or a Postgres default-collation key on the utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci column sluice itself creates on MySQL), the second row replaced the first at exit 0, on MySQL-family and Postgres targets alike. The retry arms of MySQL's two plain write cores, after a reparent or storage-grow transient, dropped such a row the same way. A fresh first-pass copy uses the plain bulk path and was already loud. Affected: the idempotent writer from v0.4.0, the batched retry arm from v0.99.92 and the LOAD DATA replay from v0.113.0, all through v0.159.0.

- Two kinds of Postgres key went unchecked on a MySQL-family target (HIGH). A key on a nondeterministic (ICU) collation merged at CDC apply and on every copy that upserts. Every named Postgres key of a backup chain written before v0.159.0 went unchecked on a cross-engine restore into MySQL. Affected: through v0.159.0.

- A prefix key (UNIQUE KEY uk (k(5))) was compared on the whole value (MEDIUM). The server matches such a key on the prefix, so 'Apple-1' overwrote 'apple-2' on a _ci target key from a _bin source. Affected: v0.159.0's guard.

- A backup segment whose window changed a key column's collation restored with rows merged on an older binary (HIGH on a downgrade, Bug 304). Such a segment is now stamped FormatVersion 13, so every older binary refuses it. The fix is not retroactive: a chain v0.159.0 captured across a key-collation change carries no stamp. Affected: chains v0.159.0 captured that were restored with v0.158.1 or older; re-restore them with v0.159.1.

- MySQL 8 → MariaDB created PAD SPACE collations, so a KEY-COLLATION-MERGE re-copy failed (MEDIUM, loud, Bug 305). See the MariaDB guide.

How to check the silent items above: the target is a row short for every merge, so sluice verify (row counts) on a quiesced pair reports a count mismatch. To find candidate collisions, group each key column on the source under the target's collation, as in the v0.159.0 item (for a prefix key, group on LEFT(k, N)). What to do: re-copy each table that mismatches.

Open in v0.159.1:

- Chain restore can merge rows from a window that changed a key's collation and changed it back (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-REVERTED-WINDOW-RESTORE; fixed in v0.159.2 for MySQL and MariaDB binlog sources, see the v0.159.2 notice). Restore arms the guard from the window's last recorded shape, which equals the target's again, so a row written under the intermediate collation can land merged at exit 0. Measured on MySQL 8.0, for a live backup stream window and for a backup incremental run made after the DDL. A sync stream resumed across such a window is plausibly exposed too; that is unmeasured. Affected: v0.159.0 and v0.159.1. Until it is fixed: after any such DDL sequence on a key, take a fresh backup full, and verify any restore spanning that window against the source (sluice verify row counts, or the collision query above).

- A drained backup stream window that changed a key's collation cannot be restored (MEDIUM, loud, KEY-COLLATION-DRAIN-NO-DELTA). A backup stream stopped mid-window writes no schema delta on its drain commit, so the collation change reaches the target only with the next segment. The drain segment's rows replay onto the old key, and every restore refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE at that segment. Nothing merges. The same lag affects any DDL in a drained window.

- A VStream segment is never stamped 13 (LOW to MEDIUM, silent on a downgrade only, KEY-COLLATION-VSTREAM-UNSTAMPED). VStream (Vitess/PlanetScale) records no collation, so a VStream window that changed a key's collation and back stays readable by older binaries, which can merge. This release does not guard it either: no key-collation check arms for a VStream source.

Fixed in v0.159.2: two HIGH silent key-collation merges in backup windows, and a loud server-id collision. Upgrading does not repair rows that already merged. Two later corrections (v0.159.3 notice): v0.159.2's loosened-window fix did nothing when no row of the table followed the loosening ALTER in the window (Bug 306, fixed in v0.159.3), and these fixes protect only chains that recorded the evidence, not a backup incremental chain written by v0.159.1 or earlier across a window that changed a key's collation and changed it back (Bug 307). The fixes add refusals that change behaviour: see KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED, COLLATION-CHANGE-UNANNOUNCED and COLLATION-NAMES-UNAVAILABLE.

- A key column whose collation was changed and changed back inside one backup window restored with two source rows merged (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-REVERTED-WINDOW-RESTORE). A key utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci changed to utf8mb4_bin, a row 'A' written beside an existing 'a', 'A' moved out of the way, and the key changed back: the window ends with its original shape and carries no schema delta. Measured on MySQL 8.0 (MINIMAL and FULL row metadata, UNIQUE and primary keys): the target held 'A' where the source holds 'a', or with the key as the primary key row 1 was gone, at exit 0. Three paths reached it, each fixed differently. Chain restore (point-in-time restore included) now releases each recorded schema version just before the first change recorded at or after it, in the source engine's own position order, so the rows written under _bin are guarded under _bin and the restore refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE with nothing of the colliding row applied. sync from-backup places no schema version between a window's changes, so it now refuses the window (KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED). A backup incremental or a warm-resumed sync start reading the window after the revert used to record only the catalog's current _ci shape; the MySQL and MariaDB binlog reader now decodes each row under the collation its row event recorded, so the schema boundary at the change carries _bin. Affected: v0.159.0 and v0.159.1, by code-reading at both tags; earlier releases have no key-collation guard and merge the same way. Corrected in v0.159.3 (Bug 307): the restore fix reaches only chains that recorded the intermediate shape. A backup incremental written by v0.159.1 or earlier that read the window after the revert recorded only the reverted shape and no schema delta, so v0.159.2 restores it, and replays it through sync from-backup, with the rows merged at exit 0; no release can detect it (details).

- A key column whose collation was loosened inside one backup window restored or replayed with two source rows merged (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-LOOSENED-WINDOW). A key utf8mb4_bin holding 'a', a row 'A' written beside it, moved out of the way, and the key loosened to utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci: the window's schema delta loosened the target key before any of its rows replayed, and nothing guarded the rows written before the change. Measured on MySQL 8.0 (MINIMAL and FULL, UNIQUE and primary keys), at exit 0, by chain restore of a backup stream rollover window and of a backup incremental, by sync from-backup over a rollover window, and by a warm-resumed sync start. Chain restore now releases, ahead of such a window, the shape the previous link recorded for the table, so the restore refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE; its message says that restarting re-applies the loosening ahead of the same rows, and names the remedy, a fresh full backup taken after the key change. sync from-backup refuses the window (KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED). A warm-resumed sync start now replays exactly. Affected: v0.159.0 and v0.159.1, and earlier releases, which have no key-collation guard. On v0.159.2 the chain-restore half armed only when a row of the table followed the loosening inside the window; with none it still restored merged at exit 0, with backup verify passing (Bug 306, fixed in v0.159.3).

- Two binlog readers opened by one sluice process could register the same replica server id (loud, BINLOG-SERVER-ID-COLLISION). On MariaDB the second registration failed with ERROR 4052 (HY000): A slave with the same server_uuid/server_id is already connected, ending that stream loudly, for example one leg of several opened together against one MariaDB source. On MySQL 8 the collision was harmless, measured: both readers kept receiving every row. No silent stall was observed on either engine. The id is now a per-process base plus a process-wide sequence, at or above 65536, and checked at stream start against the source's own @@server_id, taking a fresh one on a match; every binlog stream start runs that one SELECT @@server_id. A sibling replica's id is not visible to sluice and is not checked. There is no server-id option to configure. Affected: the id scheme dates from v0.1.0 and ran through v0.159.1; the MariaDB failure is reachable from v0.99.271, the first release with MariaDB CDC. The collision was measured on Windows only; on other platforms a finer clock makes it less likely, unmeasured. Nothing to repair: the failure was loud.

The recorded-collation fix needs a row event that records collations: binlog_row_metadata MINIMAL (MySQL's default) or FULL. MariaDB's default NO_LOG records none, so on such a source nothing is stamped: chain restore's version ordering and window-start seeding and the sync from-backup refusal still apply, but a backup incremental or warm-resumed sync start reading a reverted window behind the head has no recorded collation to carry. That case is not measured; set binlog_row_metadata=MINIMAL or FULL on a MariaDB source to get the fix. A MySQL source restored onto Postgres lands byte-exact, the Postgres key being case-sensitive.

How to check a target restored, replayed by sync from-backup, or warm-resumed across such a window: sluice verify (row counts) on a quiesced pair reports a mismatch for every merge; to find candidates directly, group the key on the source under the collation the target key uses, SELECT k COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci AS kk, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY kk HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. What to do: re-copy each table that mismatches. For a chain that spans such a window, take a fresh backup full after the key change and restore from it.

Open in v0.159.2:

- A MySQL or MariaDB window that loosened a key, with no row of the table after the ALTER, still restored merged (HIGH, silent, Bug 306; fixed in v0.159.3). See the v0.159.3 notice.

- A Postgres window observed live can still restore merged (HIGH, silent, timing-dependent, KEY-COLLATION-PG-SAME-ANCHOR). A Postgres window observed live by backup stream, with a row of the table written before a key-collation change, can still restore merged. Every Postgres schema version is anchored at the same position, so a window keeps only the shape its first Relation carried; when the reader keeps up that is the pre-change shape, the restore arms nothing for the rows written under the stricter collation, and with the key as the primary key target row 1 is gone at exit 0 (measured on Postgres 16, 1 of 3 runs; when the reader lags, the restore refuses instead). Fixed in v0.160.0: see the v0.160.0 notice.

- The Postgres twin of both fixes, read after the change (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-PG-LOOSENED-REPLAY). A Postgres key tightened (ci → "C"), given a row distinct only under the tighter collation, that row moved or deleted, and the key loosened back, replayed by a backup incremental or a lagging stream started after the change, replays under the loose collation, because pgoutput carries no collation and the reader stamps the catalog's current one. Measured on Postgres 16 restored onto Postgres with the primary key on the column: target row 1 gone, exit 0. Regraded from MEDIUM. No cheap fix exists: it needs collation history the stream does not carry. Fixed in v0.160.0 from the column's catalog row instead: see the v0.160.0 notice.

- VStream, trigger-CDC and Postgres change streams record no collation. VStream events carry none, so no key-collation check arms for a VStream source and a VStream window that changes a key's collation is not guarded on restore. The trigger-CDC sources (pgtrigger, sqlite-trigger, d1-trigger) record no schema versions, so a key collation changed and changed back inside one of their windows leaves nothing to arm the restore guard from (unmeasured). Wider than this said: with no schema versions the guard is unarmed for every change, not only across such a window (KEY-COLLATION-TRIGGER-CDC-NO-HISTORY, still open in v0.160.1; fixed for pgtrigger in v0.161.0, while sqlite-trigger and d1-trigger remain open as KEY-COLLATION-SQLITE-SOURCE-UNSTAMPED). Postgres is covered by the two items above.

- KEY-COLLATION-DRAIN-NO-DELTA (MEDIUM, loud; unchanged). A backup stream stopped mid-window whose window changed a key's collation produces a correct chain that chain restore refuses (KEY-COLLATION-MERGE) at that segment on every run (details). Nothing merges. sync from-backup refuses it with KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED.

- KEY-COLLATION-VSTREAM-UNSTAMPED (LOW to MEDIUM, silent on a downgrade only; unchanged). A VStream segment is never stamped from its window's history, because VStream records no collation, so a VStream window that changed a key's collation and back stays readable by older binaries, which can merge (details).

Postgres-source backups, until fixed: after any change to a key column's collation, take a fresh backup full, and verify any restore spanning that window against the source (sluice verify row counts, or the collision query above with GROUP BY lower(k) as an approximation).

Fixed in v0.159.3: a cancelled backup stream could commit a window ending inside a source transaction, and v0.159.2's loosened-window fix missed a window with no trailing row (both HIGH, silent). Upgrading stops new severed windows and new merges, but does not repair a chain already written or a target already restored or replayed from one. The fixes change behaviour: see KEY-COLLATION-VERSION-NAMESPACE and the rewritten chain-restore KEY-COLLATION-MERGE remedy.

- A cancelled backup stream could commit a window that ends inside a source transaction (HIGH, silent). A cancel (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM) ends the window's context and, through the same context, closes the CDC reader's change channel, and the capture loop could observe either first. If it saw the closed channel, it tried to store the window's last change chunk under the already-cancelled context: the store refused the write, nothing marked the window abandoned, and the drain committed every chunk stored before the cancel. Change chunks roll on a change count (--chunk-size, 100,000 by default) or 64 MiB, not at transaction boundaries, so when the window's last transaction spanned a chunk roll, the committed incremental held that transaction's head and ended inside it. The pgtrigger and sqlite-trigger readers, and a failed Postgres standby-status send, record the cancel as their own error, which reached the same commit by a second path. The next window re-delivers the whole transaction. On a chain already written, sluice restore refuses before applying anything with SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-SEVERED-TRANSACTION once a later incremental exists. If the severed incremental is the chain's last link, the restore only logs CHAIN-TAIL-OPEN-TRANSACTION and applies the transaction's head, a state the source never had. A sync from-backup broker that applied the severed incremental while it was the chain's tip only WARNs (CHAIN-APPLIED-SEVERED-TRANSACTION) when the next link arrives, and applies the transaction again at exit 0: a keyless row lands twice, and a key-reusing transaction is misapplied. When the window's last transaction did not span a roll, the same race committed nothing of the window instead, and the next run re-read it, so nothing was lost. By code-reading, the sources that can produce a severed transaction are those whose change stream carries transaction boundaries: MySQL and MariaDB binlog, Vitess VStream and Postgres. The trigger-CDC sources (pgtrigger, sqlite-trigger, d1-trigger) carry no transaction markers and cannot. Now both arms take the same drain, and a backstop abandons the window whenever the capture ends on a context-class error with changes it read still unstored; the abandoned window is logged at WARN as BACKUP-WINDOW-ABANDONED-OPEN-TRANSACTION, and the next run re-reads it from the parent's end. Since v0.160.0 a last flush that fails on a schema-history refusal is not abandoned this way: the stream exits non-zero with the refusal (v0.160.0 notice). A window cut inside a transaction is still abandoned, as before. Affected: v0.156.12 through v0.159.2 (v0.156.12 introduced the drain-commit this arm reaches). Severed windows written by v0.19.0 through v0.156.11 are the earlier class (who should check). How to check, if you ran backup stream on those releases on a MySQL, MariaDB, Vitess or Postgres source and stopped it by cancelling it (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, a supervisor stop): run a chain restore with v0.159.3 and look for SLUICE-E-BACKUP-CHAIN-SEVERED-TRANSACTION (a refusal) or CHAIN-TAIL-OPEN-TRANSACTION (a WARN on the final link) in its output. For a sync from-backup broker fed by such a chain, grep its log for CHAIN-APPLIED-SEVERED-TRANSACTION and compare its target with the source using sluice verify --depth sample; a keyless table holding more rows than the source is the duplicated transaction. What to do: a chain that refuses or warns needs a fresh backup full; re-copy any broker or restore target that differs from the source (details).

- A key column loosened inside one backup window still restored with two source rows merged when no row of the table followed the loosening in that window (HIGH, silent, Bug 306). v0.159.2's KEY-COLLATION-LOOSENED-WINDOW fix released, ahead of the window, the key shape the previous link recorded (utf8mb4_bin), so that the rows written under it would be guarded. A MySQL or MariaDB full manifest records its tables with no namespace, while every row the binlog recorded names its database, and the window-start version borrowed the database name only from a version the window itself recorded of the same table. A window whose last event for the table is the loosening ALTER records none, so the version was filed under kd while the rows looked up <db>.kd, the guard never armed, and 'A' replayed onto 'a' through the loosened key. Measured on MySQL 8.4 under MINIMAL and FULL row metadata, with PRIMARY and UNIQUE keys, restoring both a backup incremental window and a backup stream rollover window: restore exited 0 and backup verify passed. A version that names no namespace now takes the namespace the window's first row of the table names, and a contradicting row refuses KEY-COLLATION-VERSION-NAMESPACE. Such a window now refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE where v0.159.2 merged; restarting refuses again, and the remedy is a fresh full backup taken after the key change. sync from-backup was not affected, because it refuses such a window (KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED) from the delta alone. Postgres-source chains are not affected (a Postgres manifest names public). Affected: v0.159.2 (measured); v0.159.0 and v0.159.1 merge the same window for the reason the v0.159.2 notice gave, and earlier releases have no key-collation guard at all. How to check: on a quiesced pair, sluice verify (row counts) reports a mismatch for every merge; to find candidates directly, SELECT k COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci AS kk, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY kk HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on the source, using the collation the target key uses. What to do: re-copy each table that mismatches; for a chain that spans such a window, take a fresh backup full after the key change and restore from it.

- A chain restore's KEY-COLLATION-MERGE refusal now leads with a remedy restore can run (LOW, loud, Bug 308). It used to reuse the stream applier's remedy (give the target key the source's collation and restart, or re-copy with --restart-from-scratch), but restore has no such flag and does not resume; a re-run after altering the key starts over from the full backup and fails with LOAD-DATA-ROWS-SKIPPED (measured on MySQL 8.4). The remedy now depends on the command and the key (the four cases). The applier's own remedy, which sync start and sync from-backup run still show, now names the re-copy for each: sluice sync start --restart-from-scratch, or sluice sync from-backup run --reset-target-data --yes for a backup replay. Anything matching on the old remedy wording sees different text; the marker and error code are unchanged. Affected: v0.159.0 through v0.159.2, by code-reading. Nothing was lost: the refusal was loud.

- Correction: the v0.159.2 notes overstated which existing chains v0.159.2 protects (Bug 307). They said a chain spanning a key-collation window now refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE rather than merging; that holds only for chains that recorded the evidence. For a MySQL or MariaDB source, by lane: a window that changed a key's collation and changed it back, captured by backup incremental on v0.159.1 or earlier, is not detected by any release — the incremental read the window after the revert and recorded only the catalog's reverted shape, with no schema delta, so v0.159.2 restores it, and replays it through sync from-backup, with the rows merged at exit 0 (measured on MySQL 8.4, MINIMAL and FULL, PRIMARY and UNIQUE key; by code-reading, the same holds for a backup stream window whose reader was behind the source when it read past the revert, and for a collation change made with sql_log_bin=0 in any chain written before v0.159.2). The same window captured live by backup stream, with the reader keeping up, is detected: its schema history recorded the intermediate shape, and v0.159.2 refuses. A window that loosened a key, written by v0.159.0 or v0.159.1 on either lane, is detected from its schema delta — by v0.159.2 only when a row of the table follows the loosening (Bug 306), by v0.159.3 either way. Such a window written by v0.158.x or earlier records no collation change at all; by code-reading its restore keeps the target key at the stricter collation, so nothing merges, but the target's key then compares values differently from the source's. Remedy for a chain that cannot be checked: take a fresh backup full and use it as the base for every restore from now on; check any table already restored from such a chain against the source and re-copy it where they differ, with sluice verify on a quiesced pair or the collision query SELECT k COLLATE <the target key's collation> AS kk, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY kk HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on the source.

- A MySQL CDC stream no longer dies on a busy source with look-ahead SHOW BINLOG EVENTS … Error 1220 … binlog truncated in the middle of event; consider out of disk (loud, transient, nothing lost). The schema look-ahead runs SHOW BINLOG EVENTS … LIMIT 5000 when the reader is behind the head and has to prove a table's catalog shape. On the file the server is still writing, the row-count limit carries the read past the position it needs into the live tail, where a transaction being flushed can be only partly on disk, and MySQL fails the whole statement with error 1220. Measured on mysql:8.4 and 8.0 under eight concurrent writers: about one read in a hundred tore. The look-ahead now reads a page that tore at the active file's tail as one that ended where the server stopped; it is complete when it covers the position it needed and is re-read like any short page when it does not, so it never marks a byte it did not read as checked. It still refuses SLUICE-E-CDC-BINLOG-LOOKAHEAD-SHORT when it cannot get past the tear, now carrying the server's 1220. MariaDB (whole events only) and Vitess (VStream, no look-ahead) were not affected. Affected: v0.158.0 through v0.159.2 (sync start, backup stream, backup incremental). If your stream stopped this way, upgrade and restart it.

Open in v0.159.3:

- KEY-COLLATION-PG-SAME-ANCHOR (HIGH, silent, timing-dependent; fixed in v0.160.0). A Postgres window observed live by backup stream, in which a row of the table was written before a key-collation change, can still restore merged. See the v0.160.0 notice.

- KEY-COLLATION-PG-LOOSENED-REPLAY (HIGH, silent; fixed in v0.160.0). A Postgres key tightened and loosened back, read after the change by a backup incremental or a lagging stream, replays under the loose collation. See the v0.160.0 notice.

- KEY-COLLATION-ROLLOVER-SPLIT-DELTA-DUP (LOW to MEDIUM, loud, timing-dependent). When a backup stream rollover splits a reverted key-collation window so that the revert lands in a later window than the row it made legal, chain restore applies that window's delta before its rows, and the target's own ALTER fails with Error 1062 Duplicate entry. Nothing merges, but the failure carries no named refusal and no remedy. Seen once in four runs under load; by code-reading, v0.159.2 does the same. Since v0.160.2 the failure is reported as KEY-COLLATION-MERGE, marked KEY-COLLATION-DELTA-FAILED, keeping the target&rsquo;s error and naming a remedy; applying such a change at the end of the incremental instead, so the restore converges, is still open.

- VStream, trigger-CDC and Postgres change streams record no collation. No key-collation check arms for a VStream source, and the trigger-CDC sources record no schema versions (unmeasured), so a pgtrigger live sync or chain restore into a MySQL-family target applies every change unchecked (KEY-COLLATION-TRIGGER-CDC-NO-HISTORY, still open in v0.160.1; fixed for pgtrigger in v0.161.0, see the v0.161.0 notice); Postgres is covered by the first two entries, both fixed in v0.160.0.

- KEY-COLLATION-DRAIN-NO-DELTA (MEDIUM, loud; unchanged). A backup stream stopped mid-window, in a window that changed a key's collation, produces a correct chain that chain restore refuses (KEY-COLLATION-MERGE) at that segment on every run. Nothing merges (details).

- KEY-COLLATION-VSTREAM-UNSTAMPED (LOW to MEDIUM, silent on a downgrade only; unchanged). A VStream window that changed a key's collation and changed it back stays readable by older binaries, which can merge (details).

Postgres-source backups, until fixed: after any change to a key column's collation, take a fresh backup full, and verify any restore spanning that window against the source (sluice verify row counts, or the collision query with GROUP BY lower(k) as an approximation).

Fixed in v0.160.0: two HIGH silent Postgres key-collation merges, plus a backup format break. Upgrading stops new merges, but does not repair a target already restored or replayed with rows merged. On v0.159.0 through v0.159.3 a Postgres primary-key or UNIQUE-key column using a nondeterministic (ICU) collation could end up with two source rows merged into one at exit 0, in the two ways below. Both now refuse, with KEY-COLLATION-MERGE and the new capture-time marker KEY-COLLATION-SAME-ANCHOR. A segment that records a key collation not established for its rows is stamped FormatVersion 14, so v0.159.x refuses it instead of merging; restoring a chain that contains one needs v0.160.0 or later.

- A Postgres key whose collation was tightened and loosened back no longer restores or applies with two source rows merged (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-PG-LOOSENED-REPLAY). pgoutput carries no collation, so the reader reads a column's collation from the catalog when it meets the table's relation message, which gives the collation in force now. Take a nondeterministic key, tighten it (ci → "C"), write 'A' beside 'a', move or delete it, and loosen the key back to ci: a reader replaying that sequence after the loosening read ci for every row of it, so the guard took 'A' for a re-delivery of 'a', the upsert overwrote 'a', and the replayed UPDATE or DELETE took the merged row away. Measured on Postgres 16 through a backup incremental started after the revert and chain-restored onto Postgres: row 1 was gone at exit 0. This is wider than first filed: when the tighten, the write and the loosen shared one transaction, a live Postgres → Postgres sync start merged too, at every entry (cold start, live, warm resume and --schema-changes=refuse), because pgoutput decodes a transaction at its commit, when the catalog already says ci. The fix uses the column's pg_attribute row, which altering the column rewrites: when that row's xmin is newer than, or equal to, the transaction being decoded and the collation is nondeterministic, the reader records it as not established, and both appliers compare that key byte for byte, so a merge refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE with nothing applied. The Postgres applier's guard used to stay unarmed whenever the source's collation name matched the target's; it now compares a not-established collation as bytes, as the MySQL applier's guard already did. In a backup window, a later not-established version of a table weakens the version the window keeps, so the whole window compares that key as bytes, and sync from-backup refuses such a window with KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED. Affected: v0.159.0 through v0.159.3, every release with the Postgres key-collation guard.

- A Postgres backup stream or backup incremental window that sees a key column's collation change after a row of the table was written is now refused at capture instead of restoring merged (HIGH, silent, timing-dependent, KEY-COLLATION-PG-SAME-ANCHOR). A Postgres change stream anchors every schema version at LSN 0/0, and a backup keeps one version per table and position, so a window that wrote a row of the table, changed the key's collation (ci → "C"), wrote 'A' beside 'a' and changed it back kept only the first shape, ci. The restore then armed nothing for the rows written under "C", and row 1 was gone at exit 0 (measured on Postgres 16 in 1 run of 3, when the reader kept up; when it lagged, the restore refused). The capture now refuses with KEY-COLLATION-SAME-ANCHOR when two shapes of a table recorded at one position disagree on a key column's collation (12 of 12 runs). The remedy is a fresh full backup taken after the change, with the chain continued from it. The cost: a forward-only key collation change, in a window that already holds a row of the table, is refused too, where it used to restore correctly. Affected: v0.159.0 through v0.159.3.

- A cancelled backup stream no longer turns a schema-history refusal into an exit-0 WARN. When a stream was cancelled, the drain turned any failure of the window's last flush into a BACKUP-WINDOW-ABANDONED-OPEN-TRANSACTION WARN and exited 0. That is right for a store write that fails under a cancelled context, which the next run's re-read may not repeat, but it hid a refusal behind a clean exit and a misleading headline. A refusal from the window's schema history (such as KEY-COLLATION-SAME-ANCHOR) is a verdict on what the window recorded, not a transport failure, so the stream now exits non-zero with that refusal. Store-write failures under the cancel keep the WARN and exit 0.

- A MySQL or MariaDB stream behind the binlog head no longer refuses every table because of an unrelated statement that starts with a session SET (LOW, loud). The schema look-ahead treated a statement it could not parse as reaching every table, and a binlog text such as set foreign_key_checks=0; CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ... is two statements, so one such statement anywhere on the server made every stream behind the head refuse SLUICE-E-CDC-SCHEMA-REPLAY-MISMATCH on every retry (measured on MariaDB 11.4, where a sync target sharing the source's server created sluice's own control table that way). A leading run of plain session assignments, with no quotes, parentheses or comments before its ;, is now skipped and the statement after it classified. Affected: v0.158.0 through v0.159.3. Nothing was lost; upgrade and restart.

- A serial-apply refusal no longer logs a remedy the running command cannot carry out (LOW, loud, Bug 309). With --apply-concurrency=1, the batch-rollback WARN (batch rollback on position-write error or batch rollback on error) carried the applier's raw error, so for a chain restore's KEY-COLLATION-MERGE it repeated the stream remedy ahead of the correct one restore then printed. The WARN now keeps a transient error's text, which is retried and has no other record, and says a terminal refusal, reported by the caller in place of a terminal refusal's text. The returned refusal was right on every path, and the default lane path never logged the WARN. Anything matching on that WARN's error text will see less. Affected: v0.159.3.

Who needs to act:

- Postgres-source backup operators whose primary-key or UNIQUE-key columns use a nondeterministic collation, and who changed such a key's collation (especially tightened it and later loosened it back) on v0.159.0 through v0.159.3: a restore through a window spanning that change may hold one row where the source holds two, at exit 0. Check: on a quiesced pair, run sluice verify (row counts); every merge shows as a mismatch. To find candidates directly, run the collision query on the source, grouping the key under the collation the target key uses (GROUP BY lower(k) is an approximation for a case-insensitive key). Action: re-copy any table that differs, and take a fresh backup full after the key change as the base for future restores.

- Postgres → Postgres sync start operators who changed a key's collation and changed it back inside one transaction on v0.159.0 through v0.159.3: the live target may have merged rows. Check with sluice verify as above and re-copy (sync start --restart-from-scratch) any table that mismatches.

- Anyone running more than one sluice version over the same backup chain (for example a v0.160.0 writer with a v0.159.x restore host): once a 14 segment exists, v0.159.x refuses the chain. Upgrade every binary that reads the chain to v0.160.0 or later.

- Postgres backup stream and backup incremental operators who change key collations on live tables: expect KEY-COLLATION-SAME-ANCHOR at capture, and take a fresh backup full after the change when it fires.

Still open in v0.160.0: KEY-COLLATION-ROLLOVER-SPLIT-DELTA-DUP (loud: a rollover-split reverted window can fail chain restore with the target's own Error 1062 Duplicate entry; nothing merges), KEY-COLLATION-DRAIN-NO-DELTA and KEY-COLLATION-VSTREAM-UNSTAMPED, unchanged from the v0.159.3 notice. VStream and trigger-CDC sources still record no collation (for trigger-CDC that leaves the guard unarmed on every change, see KEY-COLLATION-TRIGGER-CDC-NO-HISTORY; fixed for postgres-trigger in v0.161.0, see the v0.161.0 notice), and sync from-backup applied every incremental unguarded until v0.160.1 (v0.160.1 notice). A Postgres DDL whose xid was assigned before, but which committed after, the replayed transaction, and a table or key column renamed or dropped after the rows, stay outside the not-established check (not covered). A chain written before v0.160.0 kept no trace of either case — a dropped same-anchor shape, or a key loosened back before the capture read its rows — so its restore on v0.160.0 cannot refuse and still merges at exit 0 (measured by the v0.160.0 regression cycle): take a fresh backup full after such a change and check targets already restored with sluice verify.

Fixed in v0.160.1: sync from-backup applied every incremental with the key-collation guard unarmed (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-BROKER-UNARMED). Upgrading stops new merges, but does not repair a target the broker already merged. The applier's KEY-COLLATION-MERGE check arms from the source's schema, which reaches it as schema versions in the change stream. A live sync start and a chain restore deliver those versions; the broker replays a chain's incrementals as source events only, so its check had nothing to arm from and stayed off for every incremental, not only one that changed a collation (the backlog had filed it as a narrow window case). Measured on Postgres 16 → MySQL 8.0, with a UNIQUE key beside the primary key on the Postgres default collation (case-sensitive), which MySQL creates under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci: an incremental inserting 'A' beside an existing 'a' overwrote row 1's key and dropped the new row, at broker exit 0, where live sync start refuses the same row. The broker now hands the applier each incremental's recorded schema before replaying it, held in memory and never persisted. That shape is sound for the whole window because the broker already refuses any window whose recorded versions disagree with it on a key collation (KEY-COLLATION-HISTORY-UNORDERED). A MySQL-family backup records its tables without a database name while its rows name one, so a seeded shape with no database name answers for its table under any (the Bug 306 trap). A broker that would have merged now refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE with the target untouched; give the target's key column a binary collation, as the message says, and restart the broker. Affected: v0.159.0 through v0.160.0. v0.159.0 introduced the key-collation guard; earlier releases have no guard on any path. Not affected: live sync start and chain restore (they already armed the guard), and broker pairings whose target key compares as the source's does.
Who needs to act:

- Anyone who ran sync from-backup on v0.159.0 through v0.160.0 into a MySQL-family target from a Postgres source, or into a target whose key columns were loosened by hand. The target may hold one row where the source holds two, at broker exit 0. Check: on a quiesced pair, run sluice verify (row counts); every merge shows as a mismatch. Action: upgrading does not repair rows that already merged. A merged table needs a target key whose collation keeps the two values apart (a binary collation such as utf8mb4_bin, which the refusal message names) before it can hold both rows again, and then its rows copied from the source. A plain --reset-target-data re-copy is not enough on its own: it recreates the key under the target's default collation, so the copy refuses KEY-COLLATION-MERGE again rather than merge.

- pgtrigger-source operators syncing or chain-restoring into a MySQL-family target: still unguarded in the same way (KEY-COLLATION-TRIGGER-CDC-NO-HISTORY, open in v0.160.1; fixed in v0.161.0, see the v0.161.0 notice). Check such targets with sluice verify.

Known issue in v0.160.1: a column named both, leading or trailing inside TRIM(…) changes meaning on a Postgres target (HIGH, silent, Bug 311; fixed in v0.160.2). v0.160.1's GitHub #356 fix kept those three words bare anywhere inside TRIM, so where a MySQL or MariaDB source used such a column as TRIM's remove-string (MySQL stores trim(`both` from `code`)), the Postgres target got TRIM(BOTH FROM code), which trims spaces. A generated column computed different values (measured: bbabb and bab where the source computed a and   bab  ) through migrate, sync start and later CDC rows, and a CHECK over the same shape became a different constraint, all at exit 0. Affected: v0.160.1 only; MySQL or MariaDB source → Postgres target; a generated column or CHECK that uses a column named both, leading or trailing inside TRIM. Check: compare the target's generated values with the source's; sluice verify --depth count does not see this, because the row counts match. Action: upgrade to v0.160.2, then re-copy the affected tables (--reset-target-data --yes for a sync start stream); a stored generated column recomputes only when its row is written.

v0.160.2: three key-collation refusals and warnings now name a remedy that works. No rows are affected by any of them; they change what the operator is told.

- KEY-COLLATION-PRE0159-2-UNVERIFIABLE (WARN, MEDIUM; Bug 307). A MySQL or MariaDB incremental captured before v0.159.2 recorded a key's collation only as of its window's end, so a key changed and changed back inside the window left no evidence, and every release restores it with the two source rows merged at exit 0. No release can refuse it, because nothing in the chain says it happened. Chain restore, sync from-backup and backup verify now log this WARN for every such incremental that records a character column in a primary or unique key, naming the table and its key columns. It is a warning; nothing refuses. Action: run sluice verify against the source for those tables, and take a fresh full backup with v0.159.2 or later.

- KEY-COLLATION-DELTA-FAILED (LOW to MEDIUM, loud). Chain restore applies an incremental's schema changes ahead of its rows, so a later incremental that loosens a key back can reach the target while two values the source had already reconciled are both still there, and MySQL refuses the ALTER with Error 1062 Duplicate entry (an hourly backup incremental splits a change from its revert this way by construction; KEY-COLLATION-ROLLOVER-SPLIT-DELTA-DUP). Nothing merges. The raw error is now KEY-COLLATION-MERGE, marked KEY-COLLATION-DELTA-FAILED, keeping the target's error and giving the remedy the other refusals of such a window give: take a fresh full backup after the key change and restore it into an empty target.

- A Postgres-target CDC KEY-COLLATION-MERGE names the table and a remedy that can work (LOW, loud). On the pipelined batch apply path, the default, the refusal named no table; on the serial path it said to give the target's key the source's collation, which cannot converge for a key compared byte for byte because its collation was not established for the replayed rows. Both paths now name the table and the collation the key was compared under ("k" COLLATE "C"), with the ALTER TABLE and the re-copy for sync start and sync from-backup; where the target already has the source's collation, the remedy offers the re-copy alone.

Fixed in v0.161.0: two ways a MySQL target's key could merge two source rows into one at exit 0, plus a backup format break. Upgrading stops new merges, but does not repair a target that already merged.

- A pgtrigger source now arms the key-collation guard on a MySQL-family target (HIGH, silent, KEY-COLLATION-TRIGGER-CDC-NO-HISTORY). The guard learns the source key's collation from the schema version the change stream carries; the pgoutput reader emits one at every table's first change of a stream, and the trigger-CDC reader emitted none. A Postgres UNIQUE key beside the primary key on a case-sensitive collation (the database default, or "C") is created on MySQL under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, and an insert of 'A' beside 'a' became an ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE onto the 'a' row, with no DDL anywhere (measured on Postgres 16 → MySQL 8 for live sync start, cold start and warm resume, and for a chain restore of a backup incremental and of a backup stream window). The reader now precedes each table's first change of a session with a schema version read from the source catalog, stamping each column's collation as the pgoutput reader does; it flows into the target's schema history and a backup's schema history like a native Postgres version (see the first-touch boundary for what that changes). sync from-backup was already guarded, arming from each segment's recorded schema since v0.160.1 (KEY-COLLATION-BROKER-UNARMED). Cost: one schema read per schema per session plus one collation query per table (measured: 100 first touches beside 500 tables, views and sequences took 1.36 s in all). backup incremental --max-changes now counts each table's version as a change, as it already did for native Postgres, so a window can close one row earlier.

- A MySQL target's functional unique key no longer lets one source row overwrite another (MEDIUM, silent, KEY-COLLATION-FUNCTIONAL-KEY-PART; HIGH, silent, FUNCTIONAL-CAST-HIDDEN-COLLATION). The guard skipped every functional key part, so a Postgres UNIQUE (lower(email)), created on MySQL under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci where lower('e') and lower('é') are one key, merged at CDC apply and on every idempotent copy path (measured on MySQL 8.4; a fresh migrate or sync cold start was already loud). And a MySQL → MySQL functional key part compares under a hidden column's collation that its expression text does not record, so a key over a charset-less CAST, a string literal, or a column altered after the key was created was rebuilt under the target default and merged rows the source kept apart (released versions are exposed too). See functional key parts.

- Backup FormatVersion 15. A backup of a vanilla-MySQL table with a collated functional key part records that hidden collation and is stamped 15, so v0.160.4 and older refuse it at their ceiling rather than rebuild the key from its text and restore with a row gone. Existing backups are unchanged.

Who needs to act:

- Anyone streaming or backing up a pgtrigger source into a MySQL-family target, where a table has a UNIQUE key beside its primary key on a case-sensitive collation. Check: compare the target's rows against the source's for such tables (sluice verify row counts on a quiesced pair shows every merge as a mismatch). Action: where the source holds values that differ only by case, the target key cannot hold both, so a plain re-copy does not repair the table: sync start --restart-from-scratch recreates the table with the same key and fails Error 1062 at the index build (measured). What converges (measured): create the target table yourself with the key comparing byte for byte (COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin), then run sync start --restart-from-scratch --schema-already-applied.

- Anyone with a MySQL-family target whose tables carry functional unique keys, especially from a Postgres UNIQUE (lower(…)) source or a MySQL → MySQL key over a CAST, a string literal, or a column altered after the key was created. Check: compare row counts and keys against the source. Action: re-copy the affected tables on v0.161.0; a KEY-COLLATION-MERGE refusal names the key to recreate.

- Anyone restoring backups across versions: restore any chain containing a version-15 manifest with v0.161.0 or later.

- Anyone downgrading a pgtrigger stream past v0.161.0: see the downgrade note.

Still open: an sqlite-trigger or d1-trigger source records no collation, so nothing arms for it (KEY-COLLATION-SQLITE-SOURCE-UNSTAMPED, HIGH, silent when reached; see not covered). Since fixed: a source DROP INDEX on a plain unique index, followed by a row duplicating the dropped key, merged at exit 0 (HIGH, silent, measured on v0.161.0; SOURCE-DROPPED-UNIQUE-KEY-MERGE). The target kept the key, so the source's next duplicate of it arrived as an upsert onto a different row. v0.161.1 added the terminal refusal UNIQUE-KEY-CONFLICT-OTHER-ROW, which refuses most such merges at the first colliding row. v0.162.0 adds SOURCE-UNIQUE-KEY-ABSENT, which compares the target's unique keys with the source's at every start and at schema changes, and every 15 seconds on postgres-trigger, sqlite-trigger, d1-trigger, PlanetScale and Vitess sources. What the two still do not catch is listed with the check.

## The control: --schema-changes

A single tristate flag on sync start (and per-sync in a sync run fleet spec) governs the behavior, introduced in ADR-0091:

Mode · Behavior ·

--schema-changes=forward (default) · Apply every unambiguous source schema change on the target automatically — ADD/DROP COLUMN, ALTER COLUMN TYPE, and, on a MySQL source, ALTER NULLABILITY — logging each applied DDL at INFO. The sync stays online through routine schema evolution. CREATE/DROP INDEX and ADD/DROP/MODIFY CHECK are not among them on any source: see the matrix below. Nor are constraint, row-level-security, policy or DEFAULT changes — since v0.156.0 those stop the stream on Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB binlog sources. Since v0.158.0 a type or nullability change is forwarded one column per boundary (two or more in one ALTER refuse), and a change to a table's column order refuses with COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED until the target holds it. Since v0.159.0 a key column's collation or character-set change met at a table's first boundary is judged against the source's earlier shape and forwarded (KEY-COLLATION-CHANGED), and on a MySQL/MariaDB binlog source a change that leaves a column name holding a different column refuses with COLUMN-IDENTITY-CHANGED in every mode. ·

--schema-changes=refuse · Forward nothing, for operators who gate DDL through a separate change-management process. Since v0.156.10 every schema boundary is checked against the target table instead: a change the target cannot hold (a source column the target lacks, a type its column cannot take — DATETIME precision, DECIMAL scale, a longer VARCHAR) stops the stream with SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED before any row after it is applied; a target column changed ahead of the source that holds every value passes with a WARN; a source narrowing or DROP COLUMN the stream's own earlier shape proves refuses too, and on a Postgres source one it cannot place refuses as AMBIGUOUS-SCHEMA-BOUNDARY. Apply the change on the target and restart (the drained model); an ADD COLUMN you apply there is not backfilled. Through v0.156.9 this mode refused nothing the target could not hold, and type widens were rounded into the target (GC-44 F5). Since v0.158.0 a change to a table's column order is judged on the order rather than column by column, and refuses as SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED carrying COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED until the target holds it. Since v0.159.0 a key column's collation or character-set change refuses as SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED carrying KEY-COLLATION-CHANGED. ·

The v0.99.45 default flip, stated precisely. Forwarding became the default in v0.99.45, and that release said a stream that previously refused on source DDL would now forward it. That was false for a MySQL-family binlog source, and for a change made to a Postgres source while the stream was stopped: before v0.99.45 those streams had no schema-change check at all unless --forward-schema-add-column was set, and --schema-changes=refuse had none until v0.156.10's SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED check — a column type widen was rounded into the target's old column at exit 0. (A Postgres source's reader did refuse a type change, drop or rename on a table it had already seen in the same session.) Note also that --schema-changes is a no-op under coordinated Shape A (--inject-shard-column): the multi-shard boundary router already forwards every shape via its lease. With --no-coordinate-live-ddl, Shape A forwards nothing and gets the refuse check. A pgtrigger source under --inject-shard-column must run with --no-coordinate-live-ddl since v0.161.0: it refuses live coordination at start with TRIGGER-SOURCE-LIVE-DDL-COORDINATION. The older --forward-schema-add-column boolean is deprecated — forwarding is on by default and covers every shape, so the flag is subsumed; setting it logs a deprecation warning and forwards.

## What forwards, by source engine

Under forward, the intercept can emit any shape's DDL, but a change only reaches the target if the source's CDC stream actually carries its detail on the wire. Postgres logical replication (pgoutput) carries less than MySQL's information_schema re-read, so the honest matrix differs by source engine. This is the ground-truth table from ADR-0091 §1d — do not assume a shape forwards without checking it:

Shape · MySQL / MariaDB source · Postgres source ·

ADD COLUMN · forwards, with its DEFAULT; pre-existing target rows backfilled from the source7 · forwards, with its DEFAULT; pre-existing target rows backfilled from the source7 ·

DROP COLUMN · forwards · forwards ·

ALTER COLUMN TYPE (same- or cross-engine) · forwards5 — one column per ALTER; two or more refuse (v0.158.0+) · forwards5 — one column per ALTER; two or more refuse (v0.158.0+) ·

ALTER NULLABILITY · forwards — one column per ALTER, as for a type change · not forwarded — stops the stream (UNFORWARDED-SCHEMA-CHANGE)1,6 ·

Column REORDER, or a RENAME COLUMN swap or rotation · refuses (COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED) until the target holds the new order2 · refuses (COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED) until the target holds the new order — a Postgres &ldquo;reorder&rdquo; is only ever a swap2 ·

CREATE / DROP plain (non-unique) INDEX · no boundary — never reaches the target and is not detected; mirror manually3 · never signaled on the wire — cannot forward and is not detected; mirror manually1 ·

ADD / DROP / MODIFY CHECK · not forwarded — stops the stream (UNFORWARDED-SCHEMA-CHANGE)3,6 · not forwarded — stops the stream (UNFORWARDED-SCHEMA-CHANGE)1,6 ·

PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE / FOREIGN KEY (add, drop, change) · not forwarded — stops the stream6 (a UNIQUE index counts, including a prefix-length change) · not forwarded — stops the stream6 (constraints, EXCLUDE included; a bare CREATE UNIQUE INDEX with no constraint is a plain index here) ·

DEFAULT / identity / generated change on an existing column · not forwarded — stops the stream6 (DEFAULT, EXTRA such as AUTO_INCREMENT / ON UPDATE, generation expression) · not forwarded — stops the stream6 (SET/DROP DEFAULT, identity, generated column) ·

Row-level security / CREATE/ALTER/DROP POLICY · — · not forwarded — stops the stream6 ·

RENAME COLUMN · refuses (§rename) · forwards via attnum4; a swap or rotation refuses (row above) ·

RENAME TABLE / multi-shape combo · refuses · refuses ·

1 pgoutput's relation message carries only column name + type + the replica-identity key flag — no nullability flag, no secondary-index or CHECK metadata. The wire never signals these on a Postgres source, so they produce no boundary to forward. Nullability and CHECK changes are caught by the v0.156.0 door instead (6); a plain index change is not caught by anything.
2 v0.158.0+ (ADR-0091 §4, amended). A reorder (MODIFY c … AFTER id) and a rename swap or rotation (RENAME COLUMN b TO c, RENAME COLUMN c TO b) produce the same boundary: every column keeps its name and type, and only the declared order changes. The old argument for a no-op — sluice decodes rows by column name, so a reorder needs no DDL — holds for a reorder and not for a swap, which leaves every row the target already holds under the wrong column names. So both refuse until the target's own column order has moved from its recorded order to the source's: run the same MODIFY … AFTER or RENAMEs on a target that can reorder in place (MySQL, PlanetScale, Vitess and MariaDB targets), or re-copy a Postgres target. From v0.99.45 through v0.157.2 both were forwarded as a no-op (see the v0.158.0 notice).
3 MySQL's CDC projection reads only {schema, name, columns, primary key} on a DDL boundary; it does not project secondary indexes or CHECK constraints. An index-only or CHECK-only DDL therefore produces no boundary at all and is never forwarded. For a plain index that is still the whole story — it is not refused and nothing is logged about it; the change simply never reaches the target, and you add it there out-of-band. A CHECK change, since v0.156.0, is caught by the door in 6 on a binlog source. Forwarding either would need a new catalog projection (perf-only for indexes; cross-engine expression-translation-hazardous for checks), so both are deferred.
4 A Postgres RENAME is proven via the stable pg_attribute.attnum — see RENAME COLUMN.
5 With two carve-outs, both below: a cast to or from a session-normalised timestamp always refuses (session-normalised timestamp), and on a Postgres source a change your projected type cannot express refuses under both modes (projection-invisible changes).
6 v0.156.0+, Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB binlog sources. Neither change stream describes these objects, so they never forward; through v0.155.1 they were dropped with no log line and the target stayed weaker than the source. Now the stream stops at the next write to that table with UNFORWARDED-SCHEMA-CHANGE, the refusal is recorded, and every later start refuses again until acknowledged — see below. Not covered: PlanetScale / Vitess (VStream) sources, where these changes are still silent, and the trigger-CDC engines (postgres-trigger, sqlite-trigger, d1-trigger), whose own readers this door does not reach (for postgres-trigger's DDL handling see below).
7 v0.156.1+. The column's DEFAULT is carried on the target's ADD COLUMN: a MySQL/MariaDB binlog source carries it in-band, and on a Postgres or PlanetScale/Vitess source — whose change streams have no field for it — the forward reads it through the source schema reader, the same value a cold-start migrate emits, and refuses if that read fails (through v0.156.0 it was dropped, so the target filled its pre-existing rows with NULL, NOT NULL columns included). The DEFAULT is read when the boundary reaches sluice, though, so it can differ from what the source filled its own rows with — hence the backfill, on by default. A non-constant DEFAULT the source still declares at that point refuses. The same applies under Shape A (--inject-shard-column). Toward a MySQL-family target a TEXT/BLOB/JSON/GEOMETRY DEFAULT that cannot be carried refuses the ADD COLUMN (LOB-DEFAULT-NOT-CARRIED).

Every forwarded DDL is logged at INFO as it lands, so the applied change is visible in the sync's log stream. Cross-engine type ALTERs are retargeted through the same translation path a cold-start CREATE TABLE uses; a widening ALTER forwards cleanly, while a narrowing or incompatible one is rejected by the target engine and surfaces as a loud, retryable refuse (position not advanced).

## What always refuses, even under forward

These shapes never auto-apply, because forwarding them would silently change or lose stored data:

### A cast to or from a session-normalised timestamp

An ALTER COLUMN TYPE where either side is a session-normalised timestamp — MySQL TIMESTAMP, Postgres timestamptz — refuses, in either direction and at any precision. Those types store UTC, so the server has to resolve them through the executing session's zone to render them as anything else (and to read anything else into them), and nothing on the binlog or the pgoutput wire carries which zone that was. The source operator's ALTER ran under their own session — MySQL's shipped default is time_zone=SYSTEM, the host zone — while sluice pins UTC on every connection it opens, so forwarding the same statement re-casts the target's pre-existing rows against a different zone. Row counts stay equal, every row applied after the ALTER is correct, and the sync exits 0: exactly the silent shape the refusals on this page exist for.

The original refusal was the TIMESTAMP ↔ DATETIME swap alone. Since v0.139.0 it covers the wider measured class. On MySQL 8.0.46 and PostgreSQL 16, a value stored at 2026-06-15 20:00:00 UTC and altered under a +09:00 session read back as 2026-06-16 05:00:00 through VARCHAR, 2026-06-16 through DATE (across midnight), 05:00:00 through TIME and 20260616050000 through BIGINT; the reverse casts into TIMESTAMP shifted the stored instant by the same nine hours, and PG timestamptz to text / date behaved identically. All of them forwarded unrefused before. The time and timetz pair is MEASURED asymmetric, and since v0.142.0 the refusal matches the measurement instead of covering both halves. time to timetz is session-dependent and still refuses: an offset is invented, and Postgres takes it from the executing session. timetz to time is not, and now forwards — timetz stores its offset alongside each value, so dropping it consults no session zone, measured byte-identical under UTC and Asia/Tokyo across negative and fractional offsets, 1-D arrays with NULL elements, and 2-D arrays checked with array_dims. Before v0.142.0 that direction was refused too, halting a stream you would expect to forward. The array shapes follow the scalars (time[] to timetz[] refuses, timetz[] to time[] forwards), and the timestamp family is unchanged and still refuses both ways, because timestamptz is stored normalised to UTC and re-renders through the session zone whichever way the cast runs. A precision-only change within one type (DATETIME(3) → DATETIME(6)) and a cast with no zoned side at all (DATETIME → VARCHAR) carry no zone conversion and keep forwarding.

Scope, stated precisely. The widened class is enforced at the pipeline door, which is reached when a boundary is forwarded — the mode that re-casts the target's existing rows, and so where the widening does its work. The reader-side checks that refuse at a table's first boundary after a cold start or a warm resume still carry only the original TIMESTAMP/DATETIME pair. Either way the remedy is the drained model below: stop with --wait, run the same ALTER on source and target from your own client so both casts happen under a session zone you chose, then restart with the same --stream-id.

### RENAME COLUMN

A column rename and a DROP x + ADD y of the same type are indistinguishable from the replication stream alone — both present as exactly one dropped column and one added column. Guessing RENAME when the truth is drop+add keeps stale data under the new name; guessing drop+add when the truth is RENAME drops the column's data on the target. The only safe disambiguation is a stable column identity that survives a rename:

- Postgres has one — pg_attribute.attnum is stable across a rename. The PG CDC reader carries it as the column's stable id; the intercept forwards a rename only when the before and after columns share the same non-zero attnum (proven rename, data preserved) and refuses otherwise. Because the proof is definitive, a bug here can only ever refuse safely, never mis-forward.

- MySQL has no equivalent — ORDINAL_POSITION changes on reorder and there is no creation id, so a MySQL-source rename is fundamentally unprovable from catalog state. It refuses, permanently. Drain and rename on both ends explicitly.

### ADD COLUMN with a computed / volatile DEFAULT

An ADD COLUMN whose DEFAULT is a non-deterministic function is refused, because evaluating it in the target's session diverges from the per-row values the source already inserted (ADR-0058 §2a). The refused functions include NOW() / CURRENT_TIMESTAMP / clock_timestamp(), nextval(), gen_random_uuid(), random(), and MySQL's UUID() / RAND() — matched schema-qualified or bare, and detected even when wrapped (e.g. COALESCE(NULL, NOW())). A constant DEFAULT forwards normally. If the probe of a column's default can't be read at all, sluice refuses on uncertainty rather than risk a wrong value.

The refusal looks at the DEFAULT the source still declares when the ADD COLUMN reaches sluice. A volatile DEFAULT that was dropped or changed before then — Django's AddField drops its default in the very next statement — is not refused: the forward carries whatever the source declares at that point, and the added-column backfill (on by default since v0.156.1) then overwrites the target's pre-existing rows with the values the source actually filled them with. Through v0.156.0, without the opt-in backfill, those rows kept the target's own fill. Since v0.156.1 the Shape A router (--inject-shard-column) applies the same refusal; before, on a MySQL-family source, it forwarded such a DEFAULT and every pre-existing row got the target's own evaluation of it.

### A change your projected type cannot express (Postgres source)

A consumer of pgoutput holds two representations of a column's type — the raw wire pair (type OID, typmod) and the projected IR type sluice maps engines into — and they can disagree about whether anything changed. interval precision/field restrictions and array-element modifiers are visible to the raw compare and vanish in projection, so the change classifies and there is no projected boundary to forward, while the source has already rewritten every stored value underneath it. Since v0.132.1 a detected change whose projected type is unchanged refuses under both modes, per column and keyed on column name (a middle-column DROP shifts every later ordinal, and pgoutput coalesces DML-quiet back-to-back DDL into one relation message of final state), with a catalog-derived enumeration gate holding the class closed. The refusal text is shape-aware: the two catalog-only shapes PostgreSQL applies without a rewrite — an unbounded varchar↔text swap, and an interval precision widening with the same range bits — say so instead of warning about divergence that did not happen.

### More than one column's type or nullability in one ALTER

v0.158.0+. Forward mode forwards one column's type or nullability change per boundary. Two or more columns changing in one statement — ALTER TABLE t ALTER b TYPE numeric(12,4), ALTER c TYPE numeric(12,4), or two MODIFYs in one MySQL statement — now refuse, naming every column. That includes two widens within one family, such as two VARCHAR widens. Through v0.157.2 the classifier read such a change as no change at all: a Postgres target kept numeric(10,2) and rounded every later value (1.2345 landed as 1.23, at exit 0, measured), while a MySQL target refused the first value that did not fit with DECIMAL-SCALE-EXCEEDED. Against the cold-start seed the target decides, as it does for one column, and at the first boundary after a cold start several nullability-only changes are skipped with a WARN, as a single one is. Recover with the drained model, applying every change on the target, or issue the changes as separate ALTER statements.

### A change to a table's column order: COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED

v0.158.0+, every schema-changes mode. A column swap (RENAME COLUMN b TO c, RENAME COLUMN c TO b), a rotation of three or more names, and a MySQL/MariaDB reorder (MODIFY c … AFTER id / FIRST) produce the same schema boundary: every column keeps its name and its type, and only the order the source declares them in changes. A reorder needs nothing on the target. A swap leaves every row the target already holds under the wrong column names. A boundary across which two of a table's columns changed order now stops the stream with COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED, naming those columns, before the boundary is recorded or any row after it is applied. On a Postgres source, DROP COLUMN b, RENAME COLUMN c TO b also refuses now, rather than reading as a plain drop.

The boundary is accepted once the target's own column order has moved from the order sluice recorded for that table to the source's new one, which is what applying the same change there does. A target that merely already declares the new order proves nothing. The record lives in the control table sluice_cdc_column_order. The check runs on the live forward path, at each table's first boundary after a restart (so a restart after the refusal refuses again), under --schema-changes=refuse and on multi-database streams (where the message is SCHEMA-CHANGE-REFUSED and also carries COLUMN-ORDER-CHANGED), and under --inject-shard-column. The refusal is codeless and exits 1; a sync run leg that hits it is marked failed rather than restarted (fleet). The message names one remedy:
